Distributed Predictive Control Barrier Functions: Towards Scalable
Safety Certification in Modular Multi-Agent Systems
Jonas Ohnemus1, Alexandre Didier1, Ahmed Aboudonia2, Andrea Carron1, and Melanie N. Zeilinger1
Abstract— We consider safety-critical multi-agent systems
with distributed control architectures and potentially varying
network topologies. While learning-based distributed control
enables scalability and high performance, a lack of formal
safety guarantees in the face of unforeseen disturbances and
unsafe network topology changes may lead to system failure.
To address this challenge, we introducestructured control barrier
functions (s-CBFs)as a multi-agent safety framework. The s-
CBFs are augmented to adistributed predictive control barrier
function (D-PCBF), a predictive, optimization-based safety layer
that uses model predictions to guarantee recoverable safety
at all times. The proposed approach enables a permissive yet
formal plug-and-play protocol, allowing agents to join or leave
the network while ensuring safety recovery if a change in
network topology requires temporarily unsafe behavior. We
validate the formulation through simulations and real-time
experiments of a miniature race-car platoon.
I. INTRODUCTION
Modern robotic systems, such as connected autonomous
vehicle fleets [1], aerial swarms [2], and collaborative indus-
trial manipulators [3], are increasing in scale and complexity,
necessitating appropriate control architectures [4]. As these
systems scale, centralized control becomes computationally
intractable, motivating a shift toward distributed architec-
tures [5]. While data-driven methods such as multi-agent
reinforcement learning have emerged as powerful tools for
achieving high-level performance in these applications [6][7],
the learned policies generally lack formal safety guarantees
and are difficult to certify. As a result, these policies are
unsuitable for direct deployment in safety-critical domains.
To bridge the gap between safety and performance,safety
filtersoffer a modular solution [8]. These filters minimally
modify a potentially unsafe candidate input (e.g., from a
learning-based controller) to ensure safety. By leveraging
model predictions,predictive safety filtershave successfully
enabled aggressive maneuvers, by enforcing safety con-
straints only when necessary [9]. Predictive safety filters,
however, merely enforce positive invariance of the safe con-
straint set, and the optimization may become infeasible due
to disturbances that drive the state outside this safe set [10].
A common remedy is to relax constraints via soft-penalty
formulations [11]. While this approach improves feasibility,

it sacrifices formal guarantees. Soft-constrained methods lack
a rigorous mechanism to ensure the system eventually returns
to the safe set, possibly leading to indefinite constraint viola-
tions. Recently,predictive control barrier functions(PCBFs)
have been proposed in the single-agent setting to extend the
feasible region while preserving both invariance (safety) and
convergence (recovery) properties [12].
While PCBFs offer a robust solution for individual agents,
maintaining these benefits in multi-agent systems with dis-
tributed learning-based control architectures remains a sig-
nificant challenge. Issues of infeasibility are further com-
pounded by the modularity of modern multi-agent systems,
in which subsystems may join, leave, or reconfigure during
operation. Classical approaches address the challenge of
varying topology by steering the system to a specific steady
state before allowing reconfiguration [13]. However, this
approach is time-consuming and diverts the system from its
primary operation. On the other hand, existing distributed
predictive safety filters [14], [15], [16] or controllers [17]
may fail during modular network reconfiguration because the
corresponding optimization problems become infeasible.
These limitations highlight a need for recoverable safety:
safety notions that not only ensure invariance of the safe set
but also guarantee convergence back to it. To address this
open challenge, we propose a novel PCBF-based approach
for multi-agent systems. We address the safety-performance
gap in multi-agent systems by developing adistributed
predictive control barrier function (D-PCBF)framework.
Our approach certifies both invariance and convergence using
only local information exchange. The specific contributions
are: 1) We introducestructured CBFs (s-CBFs)(see Fig. 1),
a novel formulation that enables permissive global safety
recovery using only local neighbor information. 2) We ef-
fectively enlarge the offline computed safe set and region of
attraction of the s-CBFs using an online D-PCBF distributedarXiv:2603.29560v1  [eess.SY]  31 Mar 2026

optimization that serves as a less conservative safety and
recovery certificate. 3) We design aPlug-and-Play (PnP)
protocolthat leverages the slack variables from the D-
PCBF to certify the admission or removal of agents online
without requiring the system to disrupt its operation. 4) We
validate the framework in simulation and on areal-time
miniature vehicle platoon, demonstrating that our D-PCBF
successfully filters unsafe inputs from aggressive controllers
and ensures collision-free recovery during high-speed plug-
and-play maneuvers where existing approaches would fail.
Section II details the general problem formulation. Sec-
tion III introduces s-CBFs and defines the D-PCBF, before
Section IV outlines the PnP protocol. After the synthesis
of s-CBFs for linear systems is described in Section V-A,
simulation and real-time experimental results are presented
in Section V-B. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper.

IV. PLUG-AND-PLAY PROTOCOL
In distributed control architectures for multi-agent sys-
tems, network topological uncertainty poses a major chal-
lenge to safe operation. This section develops a certifiablePnP procedure for topology-varying multi-agent systems
controlled via the D-PCBF mechanism introduced in Sec-
tion III. Even when individual agents violate constraints
immediately after a PnP operation, the proposed procedure
guarantees that the network converges to a safe operating
state. The protocol performs a single D-PCBF solve with re-
synthesized terminal s-CBFs (for the affected neighborhood),
and makes an accept/reject decision based on two certificates:
(i) a violation certificate (using predetermined bounds on
allowed state constraint violations) ensuring that temporary
violations remain within user-specified bounds, and (ii) a
recovery certificate ensuring convergence back to the safe
setS DPB.

V. IMPLEMENTATION AND RESULTS
In this section, we will first show methods of how to syn-
thesize s-CBFs for linear distributed systems. Then, we will
show results of using the D-PCBF framework in simulation
and on real miniature cars.
A. Synthesis of s-CBFs for Linear Systems
In this section, we describe distributed methods to syn-
thesize s-CBFs. We focus here on two constructive synthesis
approaches for linear systems subject to polytopic state and
input constraints: one in which the origin is the safe set, and
one in which agents compute ellipsoidal safe sets. While
the former approach follows from synthesizing structured
control Lyapunov functions as in [17], it yields the smallest
safe set. On the other hand, the latter yields possibly larger
safe sets, but requires an iterative construction method due
to nonconvexity. While it is possible to synthesize barrier
functions for general nonlinear systems (e.g., via sum-of-
squares techniques or learning-based methods [21]), this
remains computationally intensive compared with the fol-
lowing scalable, efficient synthesis for linear systems.

certificate (Line 5) would have held in both plug-in scenarios,
we did not enforce Assumption IV .2 in the synthesis of the s-
CBFs. Although we have omitted Algorithm 1 here, it would
allow us to accommodate varying levels of risk aversion and
formally guarantee safety recovery.
In addition to this experiment, which involved high-speed
plug-in behavior, we have performed plug-ins from standstill
and plug-outs of cars at various positions within the platoon.
Videos of the experiments accompany this manuscript.1
RemarkV .1 (Distributed implementation).In these hardware
experiments, because of the small number of agents, central-
ized solvers were used to validate theformulation. In a real-
world deployment, the achievable control frequency would
depend on solver convergence speed and network bandwidth,
a typical trade-off in distributed optimization [30].
VI. CONCLUSION
This paper proposes a distributed safety-filter framework
based on predictive control barrier functions for multi-agent
systems. A distributed optimization combines local s-CBFs
into a terminal constraint, and the resulting optimal value
function serves as a CBF for the overall network. This
construction yields network-level forward invariance and
convergence to a safe set after temporary constraint viola-
tions. It further underpins a plug-and-play protocol that uses
a slack-based admissibility check based solely on neighbor
information, enabling safe admission and removal of agents
without requiring preparatory system behavior. Validation

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary:
This document introduces a novel framework called Distributed Predictive Control Barrier Functions (D-PCBFs) to address safety challenges in modular multi-agent systems with distributed control architectures. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem:** Existing distributed control methods, especially those using learning-based approaches, lack formal safety guarantees, which is critical for safety-critical applications. Furthermore, systems with varying network topologies (agents joining or leaving) pose significant challenges for maintaining safety.
*   **Proposed Solution:** The paper proposes a multi-agent safety framework using "structured control barrier functions" (s-CBFs) augmented into a "distributed predictive control barrier function" (D-PCBF).
*   **Key Features of D-PCBFs:**
    *   **Predictive Safety:** Uses model predictions to guarantee recoverable safety at all times.
    *   **Structured CBFs (s-CBFs):** A new formulation that allows for permissive global safety recovery using only local neighbor information. This enables agents to temporarily violate local safety conditions if it helps in the recovery of other agents, while still ensuring overall system safety.
    *   **Enlarged Safe Region:** Employs an online distributed optimization to enlarge the offline computed safe set and region of attraction.
    *   **Plug-and-Play (PnP) Protocol:** A protocol that allows agents to join or leave the network dynamically without disrupting system operation, leveraging slack variables from the D-PCBF optimization.
*   **Benefits:** The approach aims to provide a formal, yet permissive, plug-and-play protocol for scalable safety certification in multi-agent systems. It ensures both invariance (safety) and convergence (recovery) back to safe states.
*   **Validation:** The framework is validated through simulations and real-time experiments on a miniature race-car platoon, demonstrating its effectiveness in filtering unsafe inputs and ensuring collision-free recovery during dynamic network reconfigurations.

structure.title: PROBLEM FORMULATION
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces a framework for ensuring safety and recoverability in multi-agent dynamical systems, particularly focusing on scenarios involving plug-and-play (PnP) operations. The main points covered are:

*   **Less Conservative Safety Certificates:** The work proposes an optimization-based approach that serves as a less conservative safety and recovery certificate compared to existing methods.
*   **Plug-and-Play (PnP) Protocol:** A PnP protocol is designed to manage the admission or removal of agents online without disrupting the system's operation. This protocol leverages slack variables from a Distributed Predictive Control Barrier Function (D-PCBF).
*   **Validation:** The framework is validated through simulations and experiments on a real-time miniature vehicle platoon, demonstrating its effectiveness in filtering unsafe inputs and ensuring collision-free recovery during high-speed PnP maneuvers where other approaches fail.
*   **Structured Control Barrier Functions (s-CBFs):** The document introduces s-CBFs, which allow for local relaxations of safety conditions. This enables individual agents to temporarily increase their constraint violation if it helps in the recovery of coupled unsafe agents, while still ensuring overall network-level safety.
*   **Distributed Predictive Control Barrier Functions (D-PCBFs):** The core of the framework is the D-PCBF, which embeds s-CBFs into a distributed optimization problem. This approach aims to enlarge the safe region and domain of the system by predicting state evolution towards the safe set.
*   **Problem Formulation:** The general problem of multi-agent dynamical systems with coupled subsystems, local constraints, and bidirectional communication is formulated.
*   **Control Barrier Functions (CBFs):** The concept of CBFs is defined, explaining how they encode recoverable safety by ensuring control invariance and a guarantee of convergence to a safe set.
*   **Safety Filter:** A safety filter is described, which projects the input from a performance-oriented controller onto the set of safe inputs defined by the CBF constraints.
*   **D-PCBF Optimization:** The D-PCBF optimization problem is presented, which is solved in parallel with a distributed learning-based controller. The resulting optimal slack values are then used in a distributed predictive safety filter.
*   **Network-Level CBF from s-CBFs:** A theorem is presented demonstrating that a sum of local s-CBFs can indeed form a network-level CBF, provided an initial s-CBF upper bound assumption is met.
*   **Enlarging Safe Sets with D-PCBFs:** The D-PCBF approach is shown to enlarge the effective safe set and domain compared to s-CBFs alone, by incorporating predictive optimization.

structure.title: DISTRIBUTED PREDICTIVE CONTROL BARRIER FUNCTIONS (D-PCBFS)
structure.summary: The document discusses a framework for ensuring safety in multi-agent systems using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs). It introduces "s-CBFs" (single-agent CBFs) which, while not individually sufficient for safety, can be combined to form a network-level CBF. This network-level CBF is proven to be valid under an initial state assumption. The document then proposes "Distributed Predictive Control Barrier Functions" (D-PCBFs) as a method to enlarge the safe set and domain of these CBFs. D-PCBFs involve a predictive optimization problem solved in parallel with local controllers, aiming to ensure forward invariance and attractiveness of the safe set. The D-PCBF optimization problem and a subsequent distributed safety filter are presented, along with their mathematical formulations. The goal of D-PCBFs is to enable stabilization of a larger safe set by predicting state evolution and filtering control inputs.

nodes.title: Distributed PCBF Formulation
nodes.summary:
The document introduces a framework for ensuring safety and recoverability in multi-agent dynamical systems, particularly focusing on scenarios with dynamic network topologies. The main points covered are:

*   **Structured Control Barrier Functions (s-CBFs):** A novel approach that relaxes individual agent safety conditions to allow for temporary constraint violations, enabling better coordination and recovery within the entire system. This is achieved by introducing relaxation functions that permit local increases in s-CBF values, provided the network-level s-CBF strictly decreases.
*   **Distributed Predictive Control Barrier Functions (D-PCBFs):** An extension of s-CBFs that uses predictive optimization to enlarge the safe set and region of attraction. D-PCBFs embed s-CBFs as constraints within a distributed optimization problem, predicting future states and optimizing slack variables to manage constraint violations and ensure forward invariance and attractiveness of the safe set.
*   **Plug-and-Play (PnP) Protocol:** A mechanism designed to handle dynamic changes in the multi-agent system's topology (agents joining or leaving). This protocol leverages the slack variables from the D-PCBF to certify the admission or removal of agents online without disrupting ongoing operations. It relies on two certificates: a violation certificate to ensure temporary constraint violations remain within user-defined bounds, and a recovery certificate to guarantee convergence back to the safe set.
*   **Problem Formulation and Theoretical Guarantees:** The document formally defines the problem of recoverable safety using Control Barrier Functions (CBFs) and then proves that the proposed s-CBFs and D-PCBFs satisfy these safety requirements. It demonstrates that the network-level candidate CBF constructed from s-CBFs is indeed a CBF, and that the D-PCBF optimization yields a CBF with an enlarged safe set and region of attraction.
*   **Validation:** The framework is validated through simulations and experiments on a real-time miniature vehicle platoon, showing its effectiveness in filtering unsafe inputs and ensuring collision-free recovery during high-speed plug-and-play maneuvers where existing methods fail.

The document is structured to first introduce the general problem and CBF definitions, then detail the s-CBF and D-PCBF frameworks, and finally present the PnP protocol and experimental results.

nodes.title: Certificates and Algorithm
nodes.summary:
This document section introduces and develops a framework for distributed predictive control barrier functions (D-PCBFs) for multi-agent systems. The main points covered are:

1.  **s-CBFs (Social-CBFs):** It defines s-CBFs as a local notion of safety for individual agents, which are not necessarily CBFs themselves but can be combined to form a network-level CBF. These s-CBFs allow for relaxation functions that permit temporary increases in their values, enabling agents to increase their s-CBF values if necessary for overall system safety.

2.  **Network-level CBF from s-CBFs:** It proves that a sum of individual s-CBFs forms a valid network-level CBF, provided an initial upper bound assumption on the sum of s-CBFs is met. This establishes a global safe set and region of attraction for the entire system.

3.  **Distributed Predictive Control Barrier Functions (D-PCBFs):** This section introduces D-PCBFs as a method to enlarge the safe set and region of attraction beyond what is achievable with simple s-CBFs. D-PCBFs use predictive optimization to anticipate future state evolution and ensure the system converges to the safe set. The D-PCBF optimization problem is formulated to minimize constraint violations over a prediction horizon.

4.  **D-PCBF Control Loop:** A control loop architecture is presented where local controllers propose inputs, and a distributed predictive safety filter, guided by the D-PCBF optimization, filters these inputs to ensure safety.

5.  **Synthesis of s-CBFs for Linear Systems:** The document outlines constructive methods for synthesizing s-CBFs for linear time-invariant multi-agent systems with polytopic state and input constraints. Two approaches are discussed: one where the origin is the safe set, and another using ellipsoidal safe sets to potentially enlarge the safe region.

6.  **Plug-and-Play (PnP) Protocol:** A certifiable PnP procedure is developed for topology-varying multi-agent systems using the D-PCBF mechanism. This protocol allows agents to join or leave the network while guaranteeing convergence to a safe operating state, even if temporary constraint violations occur. It relies on a violation certificate and a recovery certificate.

nodes.title: Simulation Results and Experiments
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt details a distributed safety-filter framework using predictive control barrier functions (PCBFs) for multi-agent systems. The core of the framework involves solving an optimization problem (12) to maximize a "safe set" and a "terminal region of attraction" by minimizing a log-determinant term and satisfying various constraints related to system dynamics, state, and input. This optimization problem is non-convex and is solved approximately using a distributed block-coordinate descent (alternating minimization) scheme. The constraints are designed to respect the network topology, allowing for distributed optimization techniques like ADMM.

The document then presents simulation results and experiments to validate the proposed D-PCBF architecture, focusing on a vehicle platooning example. This validation includes:

1.  **Car Platoon Synthesis:** Synthesizing safety-critical barrier functions (s-CBFs) for the longitudinal dynamics of a platoon of vehicles, demonstrating the expansion of the safe set and terminal region of attraction.
2.  **Scalability Analysis (Simulation):** Evaluating the framework's scalability by simulating a platoon under adversarial conditions (unsafe acceleration commands). It compares the solve times of centralized and distributed implementations, showing favorable scalability for the distributed approach.
3.  **Real-time Miniature Race Car Platoon:** Conducting hardware experiments on miniature race cars to demonstrate real-world robustness. This involves a decentralized longitudinal controller proposing unsafe inputs, which are then filtered by the D-PCBF. The experiments showcase the framework's ability to recover to safe operation even after temporary constraint violations, highlighting its effectiveness in scenarios where centralized methods might become infeasible.

The conclusion emphasizes the distributed nature of the framework, its ability to achieve network-level forward invariance and convergence to a safe set, and its support for a plug-and-play protocol for agent admission and removal.

structure.title: CONCLUSION
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt discusses a distributed safety-filter framework based on predictive control barrier functions (D-PCBFs) for multi-agent systems, specifically focusing on vehicle platooning. The main points covered are:

*   **Simulation Results:** The document presents simulation results for a vehicle platoon model, illustrating state space trajectories and comparing the solve times of a centralized solver versus a distributed implementation. The distributed approach shows favorable scalability, with solve times remaining approximately constant as the number of agents increases, unlike the centralized solver.
*   **Real-time Miniature Race Car Platoon Experiment:** A physical experiment using miniature race cars is described to demonstrate the robustness and online Plug-and-Play (PnP) operation of the D-PCBF formulation. This experiment involves a decentralized longitudinal controller proposing unsafe inputs that are then filtered by the D-PCBF.
*   **Key Experiment Scenarios:** The experiment includes high-speed join maneuvers (end-of-queue scenarios) and plug-out/plug-in events for vehicles within the platoon. These scenarios are designed to induce unsafe conditions, such as temporary violations of distance and velocity constraints.
*   **Framework Effectiveness:** The results from both simulations and the physical experiment demonstrate that the D-PCBF framework enables recovery to safe operation even after temporary constraint violations. It is highlighted that the distributed formulation is more robust and scalable than centralized MPC or standard predictive safety filters in such scenarios.
*   **Plug-and-Play Protocol:** The paper introduces a PnP protocol that allows for the safe admission and removal of agents without requiring specific preparatory system behavior, relying on a slack-based admissibility check based on neighbor information.
*   **Conclusion and Future Work:** The paper concludes by summarizing the proposed D-PCBF framework and its validation through simulations and hardware experiments. Future work includes deploying distributed solvers on hardware, designing less conservative terminal sets, establishing robustness guarantees for uncertainties, and extending the framework to coupled state constraints.
